Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not add a greeting, subject, signature, conclusion, or fact that the input did not supply.", "input": "At the end of the spring term, Cedar Grove School arranged the return of equipment borrowed by the seventh-grade science classes. The materials had been kept in three classrooms and the preparation room, so science teacher Mara Ellis asked each class to bring its items to the library during its regular period on Thursday. The library had more open floor space than the science rooms, and its long tables made it easier to sort the equipment by type. Ellis sent the schedule to the teachers on Monday and taped a second copy beside the library entrance. She also asked students to leave classroom-owned supplies in their usual places rather than bring them along by mistake.

The school’s inventory included 24 safety goggles, six plastic measuring cylinders, four trays of glass slides, two tabletop magnifiers, and a set of 18 rechargeable thermometers. The equipment had been checked out in September, and each class had used a paper card to record which items it took. The cards were stored in a blue folder in Ellis’s classroom. Before the return day, she compared the cards with the original checkout sheet and marked the expected quantities on a clipboard. One magnifier had been assigned to the preparation room rather than to a class, so Ellis added a separate line for it. She did not ask students to clean items beyond wiping away visible dust.

On Thursday morning, library assistant Jonah Reed placed labeled trays on the tables and put a box of spare pencils near the sign-in sheet. Ellis arrived before the first class with the blue folder and a small roll of removable labels. “Please bring the items you actually used, even if you are not sure which card they belong to,” she told the first group. “We can match them to the inventory together.” The students carried the equipment in plastic baskets, with one student from each lab group holding the door. Reed directed them to set fragile glass slides on a padded tray instead of stacking them on the table.

1. The first group checked in its goggles and cylinders. Ellis counted the goggles in pairs, then compared the total with the class card. Two lenses had smudges, but the frames were intact, so she noted the smudges without marking the goggles as damaged. One measuring cylinder was missing its printed scale near the base. The student who returned it said the scale had looked worn at the start of term; the checkout card did not mention that detail. Ellis recorded the student’s comment beside the item number and left the condition field open for review. Reed placed the cylinder in a separate tray so it would not be confused with the others.

The next two classes returned their materials before lunch. Their cards matched the expected quantities, though several students had placed the slide trays in the wrong order. Ellis checked the slide labels against the list and rearranged the trays by class. The thermometers required a different check: students brought them back switched off, and Reed tested each one using the school’s charging dock. Seventeen showed a charging light. The remaining thermometer did not respond when connected, although its casing was clean and uncracked. Ellis wrote down its serial number and the class name, then asked Reed to keep it with the cylinder for the equipment technician to inspect.

During the lunch period, Ellis and Reed compared the returned items with the checkout sheet. The blue folder contained a card for every science class, but one card had a coffee ring across the lower corner. Its item counts were still readable. They found that all 24 pairs of goggles, all six cylinders, and all four slide trays had been returned. The two magnifiers were also accounted for, including the one assigned to the preparation room. Of the 18 thermometers, 17 had passed the charging check. Ellis listed the two items set aside for inspection without changing their status on the inventory record.

The final class arrived after lunch with a basket containing a few classroom supplies along with its borrowed equipment. Ellis recognized the labeled tape dispenser and returned it to the classroom teacher before counting the remaining items. A student noticed that one goggles case had a loose hinge and pointed it out while the class was still present. The goggles inside were undamaged, but the case would not stay closed. Ellis added the case to the inspection list and explained that it was useful to report the problem even though the goggles themselves were fine. The class representative signed the return card after checking the recorded count.

Before the end of the day, Reed moved the accepted equipment to the locked storage cabinet in the science preparation room. He arranged the goggles in shallow bins, placed the slide trays upright in their protective sleeves, and set the cylinders in a compartment with a foam divider. The thermometers that had passed the charging check went onto the marked shelf beside their charging dock. Ellis put the three items awaiting inspection—the worn-scale cylinder, the unresponsive thermometer, and the loose goggles case—in a clear box on the technician’s worktable. She attached a note listing the relevant class or inventory number for each item.

Ellis returned the signed cards to the blue folder and entered the counts from the day’s checks on the school inventory sheet. She added brief notes about the smudged lenses and the student’s comment on the cylinder scale, keeping those observations separate from the confirmed inspection items. The library tables were cleared before the next morning’s reading group, and Reed returned the labeled trays to the supply closet. The science teachers received the updated inventory sheet by email that afternoon, while the three items in the clear box remained on the technician’s worktable for the next scheduled equipment review.", "output": "At the end of the spring term, Cedar Grove School arranged the return of equipment borrowed by the seventh-grade science classes.
